definition:
The Bible's teaching on marriage, family, and sexuality begins with the claim that the body and its desires are part of a good creation. God made humanity “male and female” (Genesis 1:27), blessed them, and told them to be fruitful; he joined the first man and woman so that “they will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). From that beginning Scripture honors marriage as a lifelong covenant between a man and a woman, the setting it gives for sexual union and the ordinary cradle of children. It honors singleness as well, most fully in Jesus and Paul, and it treats the household (parents, children, the widow and the orphan taken in) as the first place where faithfulness is learned. It also tells the truth about families that break: the patriarchs' rival wives, David's adultery and his children's violence, divorce, abandonment, and grief. Over all of it stands a larger story. The prophets describe God as Israel's husband, Paul reads marriage as a picture of Christ and the church, and the Bible ends with “the marriage of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:7). This study treats marriage, singleness, sexual ethics, and the household; the image of God as male and female belongs to the study of humanity, and the question of women in church office to the study of leadership.

The vocabulary is ordinary and concrete. Hebrew has no separate word for ‘husband’ or ‘wife’: ʾish means ‘man’ or ‘husband’ and ʾishshah ‘woman’ or ‘wife’, and Genesis 2:23 plays on the pair. The woman is an ʿezer kenegdo, ‘a helper corresponding to him’ (Genesis 2:18); ʿezer is used most often of God himself as Israel's help (Psalm 121:1-2), so it names needed strength, not inferiority. The man ‘clings’ or ‘holds fast’ (dabaq) to his wife, the verb used elsewhere for Israel holding fast to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20). The household is the bayit, ‘house’, and the extended clan the beit ʾav, ‘father's house’. Hebrew often describes sexual union with the verb yadaʿ, ‘to know’ (Genesis 4:1). Adultery is naʾaf, and the root zanah covers prostitution and, by extension, Israel's unfaithfulness to God. In the New Testament gamos is marriage or a wedding feast; moicheia is adultery; porneia is a broad word for sexual immorality of every kind outside marriage; and oikos is the household, including servants and dependents. Paul calls the union of husband and wife a mystērion (Ephesians 5:32), a hidden purpose now revealed; the Latin Vulgate rendered it sacramentum, a translation that later shaped debates over whether marriage is a sacrament.
ot:
Genesis sets the pattern the rest of the Bible assumes. Humanity is created in God's image as “male and female” and blessed with the command to “be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:27-28). In the second account the only thing in creation called “not good” is that “the man” is “alone” (Genesis 2:18); no animal is a fit partner, and God forms the woman and brings her to him. His first recorded words are a poem of recognition, “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23), and the narrator draws the lesson for every generation: “a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). The scene closes with a nakedness that holds no shame (Genesis 2:25). The fall touches this relationship first. Shame and blame enter together (Genesis 3:7, 12), and God's words to the woman describe the distortion that follows: “Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you” (Genesis 3:16). Interpreters differ on whether ‘desire’ there means longing or a will to control (the same Hebrew word appears in Genesis 4:7), but they agree the verse describes a broken order, not the one God made.

The rest of Genesis shows how quickly it breaks. Lamech takes two wives and boasts of vengeance (Genesis 4:19-24). Abram, promised a son, accepts Sarai's plan to “build a family” through her servant Hagar, and the result is contempt, harshness, and flight (Genesis 16:2-6). Jacob loves Rachel “more than Leah”, and the LORD sees that Leah is “unloved” (Genesis 29:30-31); the rivalry passes to their sons, who sell their brother Joseph. Genesis reports polygamy without commending it, and every polygamous household it describes is a house of grief. God's promises still run through these families, which is part of the point: grace does not wait for a tidy home.

The law of Sinai surrounds marriage and family with protection. The Ten Commandments command honor for father and mother and forbid adultery and coveting a neighbor's wife (Exodus 20:12, 14, 17). Leviticus 18 and 20 list forbidden unions, including incest, adultery, and a man lying “with a man as with a woman” (Leviticus 18:22), and set them against the practices of Egypt and Canaan. Parents are to teach God's words “diligently to your children” in the ordinary rhythms of the day (Deuteronomy 6:7). A new husband is exempt from war for a year “to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married” (Deuteronomy 24:5). Divorce is regulated rather than commended: a man who finds ‘some indecency’ in his wife may write her “a certificate of divorce” (Deuteronomy 24:1), which at least gave the woman proof of her freedom to remarry. By the first century the rabbinic schools of Shammai and Hillel disagreed sharply over what that ‘indecency’ covered (m. Gittin 9:10), Shammai limiting it to sexual unfaithfulness and Hillel allowing almost any cause.

The historical books continue to tell the truth. Ruth's loyalty to her widowed mother-in-law, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God” (Ruth 1:16), builds a new family out of loss and leads to David. David's own house shows the opposite: he takes Bathsheba and has her husband killed (2 Samuel 11), Nathan confronts him, and rape, murder, and rebellion follow among his children (2 Samuel 13 to 18). Solomon's many foreign wives turn his heart to other gods (1 Kings 11:1-4). The wisdom books teach both delight and restraint. Proverbs urges a son to “rejoice in the wife of your youth” (Proverbs 5:18) and warns at length against the adulteress; it closes with the capable wife whose husband's heart “trusts in her” (Proverbs 31:11). Psalms 127 and 128 call children “a heritage from the LORD” (Psalm 127:3), and Psalm 68 praises God as “a father of the fatherless” who “settles the lonely in families” (Psalm 68:5-6). The Song of Songs celebrates erotic love between a man and a woman without embarrassment and ends with the claim that “love is as strong as death” (Song of Solomon 8:6). Jewish and Christian interpreters have read it both as a poem of human love and as a picture of God's love for his people.

The prophets take marriage up into the story of God and Israel. Hosea is told to love an unfaithful wife as the LORD loves an unfaithful people (Hosea 3:1), and God promises, “I will betroth you to Me forever” (Hosea 2:19). Jeremiah and Ezekiel describe idolatry as adultery (Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16), and Isaiah comforts Israel with the words “your husband is your Maker” (Isaiah 54:5). Isaiah also gives the eunuch who holds fast to the covenant “a name better than that of sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5), an early word of honor for those without children. The Old Testament ends with Malachi's rebuke of men who have broken faith with “the wife of your youth” and his reminder that the LORD was “a witness” to the covenant (Malachi 2:14). Malachi 2:16 is famously difficult in Hebrew; some English versions have God say that he hates divorce, others that the man who hates and divorces does violence. Either way the verse condemns treacherous divorce.
nt:
Jesus' public signs begin, in John's Gospel, at a wedding in Cana, where he turns water into wine so that the feast can go on (John 2:1-11). When Pharisees test him on divorce, he answers by going behind Moses to creation: “from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female’”, and joins Genesis 1 and 2 into one teaching that ends, “what God has joined together, let man not separate” (Mark 10:6-9). The law's permission, he says, was given “because of your hardness of heart” (Mark 10:5). Mark and Luke record his saying that whoever divorces and remarries commits adultery (Mark 10:11-12; Luke 16:18); Matthew twice records it with an exception, “except for sexual immorality” (Matthew 19:9; 5:32). The disciples' shocked reply, that it may be “better not to marry”, draws Jesus' saying about those who “live like eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:10-12). In the Sermon on the Mount he locates adultery in the heart as well as the act (Matthew 5:28). His dealings with sexual sinners are as striking as his standard: he lets a woman known as a sinner wash his feet and declares her forgiven (Luke 7:36-50), and he speaks at length with a Samaritan woman who has had five husbands (John 4:16-18).

Jesus also relativizes the natural family without despising it. He never married. When his mother and brothers come looking for him, he points to those around him: “whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother” (Mark 3:35). He warns that loyalty to him may divide households (Matthew 10:34-37), yet he rebukes those who use religious vows to avoid supporting their parents (Mark 7:9-13), and from the cross he gives his mother into the care of the beloved disciple (John 19:26-27). He says that in the resurrection “people will neither marry nor be given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30), which means that marriage belongs to this age and points beyond itself.

Paul's longest treatment, 1 Corinthians 5 to 7, answers a church that swung between license and a disdain for sex. Against license he insists that “the body is not intended for sexual immorality, but for the Lord”, that union with a prostitute makes the two “one flesh”, and that the believer's body is “a temple of the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:13-19). Against disdain he teaches that husband and wife owe each other sexual union and that each has authority over the other's body, a mutuality unusual in the ancient world (1 Corinthians 7:3-5). He wishes that all were single as he is, yet calls both marriage and singleness a “gift from God” (1 Corinthians 7:7). He repeats the Lord's command against divorce, then adds his own ruling that a believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse “is not bound” (1 Corinthians 7:10-15). He values singleness for its “undivided devotion to the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:35) and says a widow may remarry, “as long as he belongs to the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). In Romans 1 he describes same-sex relations among the signs of a humanity that “exchanged the truth of God for a lie” (Romans 1:25-27), and in 1 Corinthians 6:9-11 he lists sexual sins among others (greed, drunkenness, slander) that exclude from the kingdom, then adds, “that is what some of you were. But you were washed”. The rare Greek word arsenokoitai in 1 Corinthians 6:9 and 1 Timothy 1:10 is formed from words that stand side by side in the Greek translation of Leviticus 20:13; its exact range has been debated in recent decades.

The household codes of Ephesians 5 and 6, Colossians 3, and 1 Peter 3 take up the form of ancient teaching on household management and change its center. Ephesians begins, “Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ” (Ephesians 5:21), then tells wives to submit to their husbands and husbands to love their wives “just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Quoting Genesis 2:24, Paul says, “This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). Children are to obey parents, and fathers are told, “do not provoke your children to wrath” (Ephesians 6:4); Colossians adds, “Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them” (Colossians 3:19). Peter calls husbands to honor their wives “as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life” (1 Peter 3:7). The Pastoral Letters condemn those who “prohibit marriage” (1 Timothy 4:3), insist that anyone who does not provide for “his own household” has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8), and charge the church to care for widows. Hebrews says, “Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4), and James defines pure religion as caring “for orphans and widows in their distress” (James 1:27). The canon closes with a wedding. A great multitude sings that “the marriage of the Lamb has come” (Revelation 19:7), and the new Jerusalem descends “as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). Every human marriage, on this reading, is a signpost, and the single and the married alike are invited to the feast it points to.

keyTexts.why: Humanity is created in God's image as male and female and blessed with fruitfulness, so sexual difference and the family belong to the good creation.
The founding account of marriage: aloneness is not good, the woman is a corresponding helper, and a man leaves his parents to become one flesh with his wife. Jesus and Paul both build on verse 24.
The Ten Commandments protect the family from both sides, commanding honor for parents and forbidding adultery and coveting a neighbor's wife.
Moses regulates divorce with a written certificate and protects a new marriage. Jesus later explains the permission as a concession to hardness of heart.
Wisdom counsels delight in the wife of one's youth and warns that adultery is folly that ensnares the one who commits it.
The Bible's love poem ends by calling love as strong as death and beyond price, honoring desire within covenant faithfulness.
God pursues unfaithful Israel as a husband and promises a betrothal in righteousness, justice, and faithfulness, the root of the Bible's marriage imagery for God and his people.
The prophet condemns men who break faith with their wives, reminding them that the LORD was witness to the marriage covenant.
Jesus grounds marriage in creation, limits divorce, and honors those who remain unmarried for the sake of the kingdom.
The body belongs to the Lord and will be raised, so sexual immorality is a sin against one's own body, the Spirit's temple.
Paul's fullest teaching: mutual obligation in marriage, singleness and marriage as gifts, divorce and desertion, and the freedom of widows.
Marriage is read as a picture of Christ and the church, with the husband's love measured by Christ's self-giving and the whole set under mutual submission.
Children honor their parents, and fathers are forbidden to provoke their children and charged to raise them in the Lord's instruction.
A compact summary of the New Testament's sexual ethic: marriage honored by all and kept faithful.
The story ends at the marriage supper of the Lamb, the reality every human marriage points toward.

history:
The early church held two convictions together that its world found strange: that marriage and the body are good gifts, and that lifelong celibacy for the kingdom is an honorable calling. An early Christian apologist, the anonymous author of the Letter to Diognetus, noted that Christians married and had children like everyone else but did not expose unwanted infants. Against groups that condemned marriage as impure, such as the followers of Marcion and the Encratites, the church defended it; a fourth-century synod at Gangra in Asia Minor (usually dated between about 340 and 355) condemned anyone who scorned marriage or treated a faithful married woman as shut out of the kingdom. At the same time the ascetic movement exalted virginity, and the balance was contested. When the monk Jovinian argued that virginity was no higher than marriage, Jerome answered him in Against Jovinian (393) in terms that seemed to many to belittle marriage. Augustine's On the Good of Marriage (around 401) took a steadier line, naming three goods of marriage, offspring, faithfulness, and the sacramental bond, a scheme that shaped Western teaching for a thousand years.

In the medieval West marriage came fully under church law. Theologians counted it among the seven sacraments, a list affirmed by the Second Council of Lyon (1274) and the Council of Florence (1439), and canon lawyers debated whether consent or consummation made a marriage. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) required banns to be published before a wedding. The Reformers kept the high view of marriage but denied that it is a sacrament of the gospel. Luther's The Estate of Marriage (1522) defended marriage as a holy calling ordained by God, and his own marriage to the former nun Katharina von Bora in 1525 made the Protestant parsonage a new model of household life. Calvin's Geneva handled marriage through its consistory. The Council of Trent answered in 1563, affirming marriage as a sacrament and its indissolubility, and in the decree Tametsi requiring marriages to be celebrated before a priest and witnesses. The Book of Common Prayer (1549) named three causes for which marriage was ordained: children, a remedy against sin, and the mutual help and comfort of husband and wife. The Westminster Confession (1646), in its chapter on marriage and divorce, allowed divorce for adultery and for willful desertion that could not be remedied, following an interpretation that Erasmus had put forward in the annotations to his Greek New Testament.

The twentieth century brought new questions. The Lambeth Conference of Anglican bishops in 1930, in its fifteenth resolution, allowed married couples to use contraception for serious reasons, the first major church body to do so; Pius XI's encyclical Casti Connubii (1930) reaffirmed the Catholic prohibition, and Paul VI's Humanae Vitae (1968) restated it. John Paul II's Wednesday audiences from 1979 to 1984, later gathered as the Theology of the Body, offered a sustained Catholic reading of Genesis and Ephesians on the meaning of the body. Among evangelicals the Danvers Statement (1987) set out a complementarian account of male headship in marriage and church, and Christians for Biblical Equality, founded the same year, set out an egalitarian account.

Since the late twentieth century the sharpest debate has concerned same-sex relationships. Some Protestant bodies in North America and Europe have revised their teaching to bless or marry same-sex couples, among them the Episcopal Church and the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) in 2015. Their defenders, such as James Brownson in Bible, Gender, Sexuality (2013), argue that the biblical texts addressed exploitative or excessive relations in their ancient setting, not faithful lifelong partnerships, and that the church has revised its reading before, as on slavery and divorce, when it saw the fruit of a teaching in people's lives. The Catholic and Orthodox churches and most Protestant churches worldwide, including most provinces of the worldwide Anglican Communion, have maintained the historic teaching that sexual union belongs within the marriage of a man and a woman. Their defenders, such as Richard Hays in The Moral Vision of the New Testament (1996) and Robert Gagnon in The Bible and Homosexual Practice (2001), argue that the texts rest on the creation pattern Jesus himself cited, that every text that speaks of the practice speaks against it, and that the analogy with slavery fails because Scripture's trajectory moves away from slavery but not away from its sexual ethic. Some who hold the historic teaching, such as Wesley Hill in Washed and Waiting (2010), write as gay Christians committed to celibacy and have pressed churches to make real room for single people in their common life. For most churches this is not treated as a second-order question, because it concerns what Scripture calls sin and repentance; this study presents the historic teaching as the church's, as the summary of this doctrine does, while stating the other case as its own defenders make it.

differ.body: The Catholic Church teaches that a sacramental, consummated marriage between two baptized persons cannot be dissolved by any human power. Its defenders point to Jesus' absolute statements in Mark 10:11-12 and Luke 16:18, to Paul's command that a separated wife remain unmarried or be reconciled (1 Corinthians 7:10-11), and to Ephesians 5, where marriage reflects Christ's unbreakable bond with the church. They read Matthew's exception as referring to unions that were never valid marriages, such as those within forbidden degrees. Separation is permitted for grave cause, and a church tribunal may declare that a marriage was never valid (a declaration of nullity), but a true marriage ends only at death.

The main Protestant confessions, following Erasmus and the Reformers, hold that Jesus' exception in Matthew 19:9 permits divorce and remarriage when a spouse has committed adultery, and that Paul's ruling in 1 Corinthians 7:15 frees a believer who has been deserted. The Westminster Confession states this view. Defenders argue that Jesus was answering the Hillel school's any-cause divorce, not abolishing the grounds already recognized, that Mark and Luke give the principle while Matthew records the qualification, and that adultery and desertion break the covenant itself. Many in this tradition extend desertion to include abuse that makes married life impossible.

differ.view: Divorce: the Orthodox way of mercy
differ.body: The Eastern Orthodox churches hold marriage to be a sacrament and ideally unrepeatable, yet by oikonomia, the pastoral application of mercy, they permit a second and even a third marriage after divorce, with a penitential form of the service. Defenders say this keeps Jesus' ideal intact while recognizing, as Moses did, that marriages die through sin, and that the church must care for the wounded rather than leave them without remedy. They note that Matthew records an exception and Paul another, which shows that the apostolic church applied Jesus' teaching pastorally to real cases.

Complementarians hold that husbands and wives are equal in dignity and worth before God and that Scripture gives the husband a loving, servant leadership in the home which the wife is called to honor. They point to the order of creation that Paul invokes, to the consistent pattern of the household codes (Ephesians 5:22-24; Colossians 3:18; 1 Peter 3:1-6), and to the analogy with Christ and the church, which they argue grounds the pattern in the gospel rather than in ancient custom. They insist that headship means sacrifice and never permits harshness or abuse, which the same texts forbid.

Egalitarians hold that Christ's work restores the partnership of Genesis 1 and 2, where rule over the earth is given to man and woman together, and that the rule of husband over wife in Genesis 3:16 describes the curse rather than God's design. They read Ephesians 5 in the light of verse 21's mutual submission, argue that kephalē (head) can carry the sense of source or origin as well as authority, and hold that the household codes adapt the gospel to ancient households without making those structures permanent, much as the same codes address slaves without endorsing slavery. They point to Paul's language of mutual authority in 1 Corinthians 7:4 and to the oneness of Galatians 3:28.

errors:
The church has rejected the teaching that marriage, sexual desire, or the body are evil or second-rate, whether in ancient forms that forbade marriage (1 Timothy 4:3) or in later habits of speaking as if the married were lesser Christians. Creation is good, the Word became flesh, and the body will be raised. It has equally rejected the opposite error, common in many ages and cultures, that sexual desire is a private matter to be satisfied as one wishes. Scripture's sexual ethic is demanding for everyone, married and single, and it ties the use of the body to covenant, faithfulness, and the good of the other. It has also rejected polygamy, which Genesis narrates but which Jesus' appeal to the two who become one flesh sets aside, and it has condemned incest, adultery, prostitution, and the sexual use of the vulnerable.

Other distortions have done great harm inside the church. One treats the family as an idol, so that marriage and children become the measure of a full Christian life and single people, the widowed, the childless, and the divorced are quietly made second-class, though Jesus and Paul were single and the church is itself a household (1 Timothy 3:15). Another uses the language of headship or submission to excuse control and abuse, which the texts themselves forbid; no reading of Ephesians 5 requires anyone to remain in danger. A third singles out some sexual sins, especially those of other people, while ignoring greed, slander, and adultery in its own ranks, and treats gay and lesbian people with contempt that has no place in a church that knows Paul's words, “that is what some of you were”. A fourth, the reverse, gives up the church's teaching in order to avoid the offense. Faithfulness requires both the truth and the tenderness that Jesus showed to the woman at the well.
life:
This doctrine reaches into the most private parts of life, and it does so with both honor and realism. It tells married people that their ordinary faithfulness, kept through boredom, sickness, and disappointment, is a living picture of Christ's love for the church, and that forgiveness is the daily work of a marriage. It tells single people that their lives are not a waiting room: they belong fully to Christ's household, their freedom can be given to God and neighbor, and the one who never married is their Lord. It tells parents that their first calling is to teach the faith in the ordinary course of the day, at the table and on the road, and to refuse the harshness that provokes children to despair. It tells everyone that the body matters, that sexual desire is to be governed rather than despised or indulged, and that there is washing for every sexual sin.

It also tells the truth to people whose families have broken. Scripture's own families were broken, and God worked through them. Those who have been divorced, abandoned, or abused, and those who grew up without a father or mother, are not outside the story; God is “a father of the fatherless” who “settles the lonely in families” (Psalm 68:5-6), and one of the ways he does so is through the church. Anyone in danger at home should seek safety and help at once, from people they trust and from the authorities; the Bible's teaching on marriage never requires a person to stay where they are being harmed. The last word belongs to the wedding supper of the Lamb, where the married and the unmarried sit at one table.
questions: Genesis 2 says it is not good for the man to be alone, yet Jesus and Paul lived and commended singleness. How can a church honor both marriage and singleness in its common life?

Ephesians 5 measures a husband's love by Christ's self-giving and sets marriage under mutual submission. How does that picture challenge both the abuse of authority and the idea that marriage exists mainly for personal fulfillment?
The Bible tells the truth about broken families, from Abraham's to David's. What difference does it make that God's promises ran through these households rather than around them?
